# Spherical Earth and its size (`round_earth_size`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, sundial_water_clock
- Core idea: The Earth is a ball about 40,000 km round (a degree of latitude is about 111 km). Evidence anyone can check: a ship's hull disappears below the horizon before its mast; the Earth's shadow on the Moon in a lunar eclipse is always round; travelling south, new stars rise and the Pole Star sinks; the same eclipse is seen at a later hour of the night further east. Its size: at noon on midsummer day the Sun stood overhead at Syene but 7.2 degrees (a fiftieth of a circle) from overhead at Alexandria, 5000 stadia north, so the whole circle is 50 times that distance. People on the other side do not fall off because 'down' everywhere means towards the centre.
- Pitfalls:
  - Telling educated people of ancient Greece, Rome, the Islamic world or medieval Europe that they believe in a flat Earth; they do not
  - Saying Columbus proved the Earth round; the dispute was its size, and he was wrong (he made it a quarter too small and Asia too wide)
  - Claiming Eratosthenes was exact to 1 per cent; the length of his stadion is uncertain
  - Forgetting that the method assumes the Sun's rays are parallel and the two places lie north-south
- History: greece: 5th c. BC Pythagoreans and Parmenides; c. 350 BC Aristotle's proofs; c. 240 BC Eratosthenes measures 250,000–252,000 stadia; india: 499 – Aryabhata: a rotating sphere, with a circumference close to the true one; islamic: c. 830 al-Ma'mun's surveyors measure a degree in the Sinjar plain; c. 1020s al-Biruni's mountain-and-horizon method near Nandana; china: a flat Earth under a round heaven remained usual until Jesuit teaching in the 17th c., despite Zhang Heng's 'egg yolk' image (c. 120 AD); mesopotamia: flat disc surrounded by ocean (Babylonian world map, c. 6th c. BC); europe: known throughout the Middle Ages (Bede 725; Sacrobosco, De sphaera, c. 1230); 1519–1522 Magellan and Elcano's circumnavigation; 1669–1670 Picard's accurate degree
- Read:
  - Aristotle, On the Heavens II.14
  - Cleomedes, On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies (account of Eratosthenes' measurement)
  - Jeffrey Burton Russell, Inventing the Flat Earth: Columbus and Modern Historians (1991)
